transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it’s these elevators, mostly the slow ones, or if I’m in a small room and the door’s locked. Soon as I step in, my chest kind of jumps, and I just get this strong need to get back out right away, before I can even think straight.
Outside of elevators or locked small rooms, do you also get this fear in other places where it might be hard to leave quickly?

Yes, mostly places like that. A little storage room, or even an elevator at the museum—places where there’s no window and the door closes tight. I know it’s not the same as being locked up, but my mind kind of treats it like trouble right away.
In those moments, is the main fear that you won’t be able to get out quickly?

Yes, that’s pretty much it. I know an elevator or a little storage room isn’t really the same as being locked up, but once I see there’s no window and the door shuts tight, my mind just treats it like I’m in trouble and I need out.
When that fear hits in an elevator or locked room, is the scariest part being trapped in that enclosed space itself?

Yes, that’s it. It’s not that I really think the elevator is the same as being locked up, but once the door shuts and there’s no window, my mind just treats it like I’m trapped. That’s the part that gets to me.
Have you ever had one of these sudden panic episodes when you were not in an elevator, locked room, or another enclosed place?
No, I don’t think so. It really seems to happen when I’m in one of those closed-in places. I can’t recall it coming on out of the blue somewhere else.
Do you get this same fear on public transportation, like buses or trains?

Not really buses or trains, no. It’s more when it’s a tight closed place, like a little storage room or an elevator, where there’s no window and the door shuts tight. Then my mind starts treating it like I’m trapped.
